answer.label: Not Abraham Lincoln — a 20th-century lumberjack saying
answer.authorDates: Earliest recorded 1944 · pinned to Lincoln only from 1960
answer.sourceLine: According to Quote Investigator ↗, there is no substantive evidence Abraham Lincoln (who died in 1865) ever said this. The line began as an anonymous lumberjack’s saying — the earliest version, from a 1944 Oklahoma newspaper, is credited to “the lumberjack” and speaks of five minutes and three minutes, not six hours and four. The Lincoln label doesn’t appear until a 1960 magazine advertisement.

source.heading: Where this line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Sooner State Press, Norman, Oklahoma, 2 Dec 1944
A lumberjack cutting a tree in five minutes would spend three sharpening his axe
A May 1960 advertisement in Roads and Streets magazine

source.excerpt: Give me six hours to chop down a tree and I will spend the first four sharpening the axe.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the earliest version to the Sooner State Press (Norman, Oklahoma) of 2 December 1944, where a minister credits it to “the lumberjack” — five minutes to cut a tree, three spent sharpening the axe.

The first time the saying is attached to Lincoln, per QI ↗, is a May 1960 advertisement — 95 years after Lincoln’s death — and even then it reads “five minutes … first three,” not the modern hours version.
QI’s verdict is blunt: “there is no substantive evidence that Abraham Lincoln … made a remark of this type,” and he “should not be ascribed any version of this saying.”
The fabrication is durable enough that in 2016 76ers GM Sam Hinkie quoted it as Lincoln ↗ in his resignation letter — and was promptly fact-checked.
source.excerptNote: The popular “six hours … first four” wording is a late, inflated form. The earliest documented versions speak of minutes — a woodsman cutting a tree in five minutes who spends three sharpening his axe — and name no famous author at all.
source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording is an anonymous 20th-century folk aphorism with no identifiable author, edition, or fixed source text — so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. It is not a Lincoln text, and the “six hours … four” phrasing cannot be tied to any single dated publication.

author.name: Abraham Lincoln
author.heading: About the man it’s pinned on
author.bio: Abraham Lincoln led the United States through the Civil War and is one of history’s most quoted figures — which makes him a magnet for feel-good lines he never spoke. His documented eloquence lives in the Gettysburg Address, his debates, and his letters; a productivity proverb about sharpening axes is not among them.

misattribution.heading: A folk saying dressed up as presidential wisdom
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook feel-good misattribution: an anonymous trade proverb about preparation, retro-fitted onto Abraham Lincoln decades after his death to borrow his authority.

items.why: Lincoln died in 1865. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no substantive evidence he ever said anything of the kind, and the earliest Lincoln ascription is a 1960 advertisement — nearly a century later.
The oldest documented forms (from 1944 onward) use minutes and name an unnamed woodsman; the familiar “six hours … first four sharpening the axe” is a later, inflated rewrite, per QI ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The kernel of wisdom is real and old — but it belongs to anonymous woodsmen, not to Lincoln, and the exact modern wording is a 20th-century paraphrase (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why it sticks to Lincoln
lead: Lincoln spent part of his youth splitting rails, and the “Rail-Splitter” image makes an axe metaphor feel authentically his — which is exactly why the saying migrated onto him. An appeal to “Lincoln said” carries far more rhetorical weight than “a logger once said,” so the attribution spread through quote sites, business books, and productivity blogs until it looked settled.
context.pull: Borrowed wisdom from an unnamed logger — not the 16th President.
